01 · About

Building things people actually use.

I'm Paul Vincent N. Villaflores, a fourth-year BS Information Technology student at Our Lady of Lourdes College Foundation, focused on full-stack web development.

I like owning a feature end to end: sketching the interface, writing the API, modelling the database and deploying it. My go-to stack is Next.js, React, TypeScript, TailwindCSS and Node.js, with PostgreSQL-style databases behind it.

My featured project, DAET Pulse, is a tourism feedback system built for the Municipality of Daet, with a public visitor side and a protected municipal desk.

03 · Featured project

DAET Pulse — Emoji-based tourism feedback system

A public feedback desk for the Municipality of Daet, Camarines Norte. Visitors leave one of four faces plus an optional note and photo — no account needed — while municipal officers moderate and analyse feedback from a protected desk.

Live demo Source on GitHub
  • Next.js 15
  • React 19
  • TypeScript
  • TailwindCSS 4
  • Zustand
  • Supabase (PostgreSQL + Storage)
  • Vercel

Design thinking process

I used the five stages of design thinking to turn a simple question — how can visitors tell Daet what their trip was like, and how can the municipality actually use it? — into DAET Pulse.

  1. 1

    Empathize

    Understanding the people the system is for before deciding what to build.

    I looked at the two groups who would use it: visitors, who are usually on a phone, in a hurry and unwilling to create an account, and municipal staff, who need feedback they can trust and sort through. I also looked at how feedback is normally gathered, such as paper forms and long online surveys, and why people skip them.

  2. 2

    Define

    Turning what was learned into a clear problem to solve.

    I framed the problem as: visitors need a way to share how their visit felt in a few seconds, and the municipality needs that feedback in one organised place. From that I set the rules for the design: no account for visitors, one tap to rate, optional notes and photos, and a protected desk for officers.

  3. 3

    Ideate

    Exploring many possible solutions before choosing one.

    I compared long surveys, star ratings and emoji faces, and chose four faces (Wow, Happy, Okay, Sad) because they are quick, work across languages and are easy to total. I then planned the features around them: places to rate, an overall-visit option, reactions and replies, and a desk with moderation and sentiment insights.

  4. 4

    Prototype

    Building a working version that people can try.

    I built it with Next.js, React and TypeScript, with Supabase for the database and photo storage. I started with the visitor flow on mobile (landing, feedback form, places), then added the municipal desk and the API routes behind both. Details such as retry-safe submissions and clear loading and error states came from building it.

  5. 5

    Test

    Trying the prototype, finding what breaks and improving it.

    I used the live site, fixed the problems I found, and wrote them up as the challenges above: failed loads that looked like empty data, photo uploads failing silently, and overall feedback that belonged to no place. Next I want to add end-to-end tests and gather feedback from real visitors and municipal staff.

Key features

  • Four-face emoji rating (Wow · Happy · Okay · Sad) with optional note and photo
  • Shared data across devices through a Supabase-backed /api/pulse API
  • Photo uploads to a public Supabase Storage bucket, confirmed before success is shown
  • Municipal desk: moderation, place management, wishes and sentiment insights
  • English/Filipino text-sentiment lexicon alongside emoji tallies
  • Layered parallax landing page with reduced-motion support
  • Focus-trapped dialogs, mobile dock navigation and safe-area spacing
  • Idempotent submissions: retries reuse the same ID, never duplicating feedback

Architecture overview

  1. Browser

    Next.js · React · Tailwind

    ↓→

  2. API routes

    Validation · rate limit

    ↓→

  3. Supabase

    PostgreSQL · Storage · RLS

The browser never talks to the database with privileged keys. Every read and write goes through server routes that validate input, then call Supabase with a server-only service role. Photos are stored in a public Storage bucket; tables are protected by row-level security.

channels ─┬─< pulses (face, note, photo, reacts)
          │       └─< pulses (replies via parent_id)
          └─< wishes (status: open | kept | burned)

API endpoints

  • GET/api/pulseLoad channels, pulses and wishes
  • POST/api/pulseSave a pulse (face, note, optional photo)
  • POST/api/pulse/reactionReact to a pulse
  • POST/api/pulse/photoUpload a photo to Storage
  • POST/api/desk/sessionMunicipal desk sign-in
  • GET/api/desk/pulsesModeration list
  • GET/api/desk/insightsSentiment summaries
  • GET/api/desk/channelsPlace management

Challenges & solutions

  • A failed database table load looked identical to an empty system.

    Each collection now loads independently and a failure returns null, so cached data survives and a retry notice appears instead of a blank page.

  • Photo uploads could fail silently after the note had saved.

    Success is shown only after the upload and the database write are both confirmed; the draft stays intact on errors and retries reuse the submission ID.

  • Overall-trip feedback did not belong to any single place.

    A reserved, protected channel holds overall feedback so existing foreign keys, replies and moderation keep working without schema changes.

What I'd improve next

  • Replace the demo reward preview with an authenticated server-side award service
  • Trained sentiment model instead of the lexicon
  • Pagination beyond the latest 500 entries
  • End-to-end tests against a staging Supabase project
